lead: Natural objects people collect—minerals, gemstones, fossils, meteorites, rocks, shells, taxidermy and other specimens, element samples and their displays—organised by what the specimen is (mineral class, gem species, fossil group, meteorite class, rock family, shell family) (mineral class → group → species, gem species → variety, taxon → locality/formation, meteorite class → official name, shell family → species), with dealers and gem laboratories in the brand register.

b.v: species/variety name per Mindat, GIA, WoRMS or the Meteoritical Bulletin
b.w: Each field values a piece by its accepted name first; mislabelled and trade-name stock is common.

b.v: exact locality and old collection labels > country only > none
b.w: Collectors price classic localities and documented provenance; locality is the main detail axis.

b.m: Natural vs treated, restored or fake
b.w: Dyed, heated, irradiated, reconstituted and composite pieces and casts must be disclosed.
CITES, ivory and protected-species laws and national export rules (e.g. fossils, meteorites) govern many specimens.

ax: Is the object a mineral, a cut gem, a fossil, a rock from space, an ordinary rock, a shell, a preserved animal or plant, a pure element sample, or something that shows specimens?
key: 1. Is it a pure sample of a chemical element (cube, ampoule, coin, crystal, periodic table set)? → Element samples
2. Is it a dome, box, jar, stand or mount made to show a specimen? → Display domes & stands
3. Did it fall from space, or form when something hit the Earth (meteorite, tektite, impact glass)? → Meteorites & impact glass
4. Is it the remains or trace of ancient life, or fossil resin such as amber? → Fossils & amber
5. Is it a shell, or the hard skeleton of a coral, sea urchin or starfish? → Shells & coral
6. Is it an animal or plant kept after death (mount, skull, horn, egg, pinned insect, pressed plant)? → Taxidermy, bones & preserved specimens
7. Is it a cut, polished or drilled stone or pearl sold as a gem? → Gemstones & pearls
8. Is it a rock of several minerals, a rock curiosity or a teaching set? → Rocks & teaching sets
9. Is it a single silicate mineral species (garnet, tourmaline, feldspar, mica, zeolite)? → Minerals: silicates
10. Is it any other single mineral species (metal, sulfide, oxide including quartz, carbonate, sulfate, phosphate)? → Minerals: non-silicates
Precedence: a cut stone leaves the mineral shelves for Gemstones; amber is a fossil even when polished as a gem; petrified wood stays a fossil; quartz and opal are oxides here, as dealers list them.
